snippet.title: How a broken heart affects your body - Roni Shanoada
snippet.description:
Dig into broken heart syndrome, and find out how grief and traumatic events can affect your body and health.

--


Losing a loved one can be one of the most traumatic experiences of a person’s life. Grief brings on a whole host of strong emotions that impact both our mental and physical health. But is it possible for these powerful feelings to endanger your life? In other words, can you actually die from a broken heart? Roni Shanoada explores how traumatic events can affect your body.

Lesson by Roni Shanoada, directed by Joana Sus, NOMINT.

snippet.title: Experience a Week in the Stone Age | Day 2: The Healer | Surviving Sickness 12,000 Years Ago
snippet.description:
A man is burning with fever, and the nearest hospital is twelve thousand years away. There are no doctors. No medicine cabinet. No word for "infection." There is only one woman — and everything she knows is stored inside her head.
Welcome to Day 2 of A Week in the Stone Age — a 7-part series following ordinary people through daily life 12,000 years ago, on the shores of a lake in what is now Yorkshire, England.
Today we follow the healer: a mother, gatherer, and keeper of a pharmacy that grows along the lake edge. The willow bark she boils this morning contains the same active compound as the aspirin in your bathroom cabinet — and she's using it eight thousand years before anyone will give it a name. By nightfall she'll break a fever, free a newborn who can't feed, and sit beside someone in the dark when there's nothing left to try.
In this episode:
→ Why willow bark was the original aspirin — and how she knew, without knowing the chemistry
→ The Stone Age tongue-tie procedure a paediatrician still performs today
→ How quarantine existed 11,000 years before anyone formalised it
→ Why these people were NOT primitive — they practised real, tested medicine
→ The chain of women, older than language, that carried this knowledge forward
→ Why the most important person in the camp tomorrow can't run, can't hunt, and remembers everything
📍 Based on real archaeological evidence from Star Carr, Yorkshire — the most important Mesolithic site in Britain (c. 9,300–8,480 BC)

snippet.title: The Real Nightmare That Inspired Open Water
snippet.description:
Imagine going on a 40-minute scuba dive in the middle of the ocean and then surfacing to discover your boat has vanished. You’ve been accidentally left behind, surrounded by endless open water with nowhere to go and no way to call for help. Panic sets in, and every minute becomes a fight for survival.

On this episode of Weird History Presents: Graveyard Shift we take a look at the terrifying true story of Tom and Eileen Lonergan, divers who were left stranded at sea and learned the hard way how a simple mistake can turn an ordinary scuba trip into a real-life nightmare.

snippet.title: New Discoveries Rewrite Maya History | Rise and Fall of the Maya MEGA Episode | National Geographic
snippet.description:
What actually happened to the ancient Maya? Mysteries unfold in this four episode Rise and Fall of the Maya Mega Episode compilation from National Geographic. Journey where the Maya lived in Mexico and Guatemala as archaeologists and historians uncover new evidence that rewrites what we know about this fascinating and mysterious ancient civilization. From the monumental discovery of a 3,000-year-old hidden megastructure to the puzzling, catastrophic collapse that forced millions to abandon their pyramid-filled cities, explore the origins of Maya power, secrets, and resilience in this documentary series. Featuring full episodes: 

Origins - 00:00 
What is Aguada Fénix? In June 2020, scientists discover Aguada Fénix, a monumental 3,000-year-old Maya structure. Uncover the hidden secrets of Aguada Fénix, the oldest monument built by the ancient Maya civilization, dating back to around 1000 BCE, that challenge everything we knew about the Maya's earliest days.

Civilization - 44:03 
New architectural and technological evidence unearthed in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula transforms long-held ideas about how the Maya civilization grew into a superpower.

Collapse - 01:28:06
Why did the ancient Maya civilization collapse? Many cities were abandoned due to a complex combination of severe droughts, overpopulation, deforestation, and warfare. The exact series of events that lead the ancient Maya to abandon their pyramid-filled cities has long puzzled archaeologists. Now, new investigations in Mexico and Guatemala are exposing surprising evidence about why these great monuments were deserted. 

Resilience - 02:12:09
Archaeologists unearth new clues about the resurgence of the ancient Maya civilization and the devastating events that would ultimately lead them to abandon their cities for good. Investigations also reveal evidence of extreme resilience in the face of catastrophe.

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Alderman (Black Death) | Day 5 of 7
snippet.description:
In November 1348, three of London's twenty-four aldermen were already dead. Two more were sick. The constables who walked the streets were dying. The clerks who kept the records were dying.

And somebody still had to run the city.

This is Day 5 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are the alderman of Vintry ward — a wine merchant turned city official who has spent nine years managing eight thousand people on the north bank of the Thames. You know every street, every landlord, every problem.

This morning your ledger has three complaints waiting. One of them is a landlord refusing to let the collection carts remove the bodies of his dead tenants. You walk there yourself. He tells you: what's the point — they're all going to die anyway. You tell him: the point is that we do the work while we can. The bodies are collected.

At noon you walk to the Guildhall. Eight empty chairs where aldermen used to sit. The Lord Mayor is still in his. The agenda: the burial ground is running over budget, seven ward constables are dead and need replacing, and the city's finances are collapsing because the port is emptying and the merchants are dying. Nobody has a solution. The meeting ends anyway.

This afternoon you sit in judgment in the ward court. A weaver hasn't paid his rent. Both his journeymen are dead. His apprentice ran home. He chose food over rent. The law says evict him. You grant him thirty days.

Your wife says it best, over supper: he's not wrong that they're all going to die. He's just wrong that it matters.

snippet.title: 🏅 What Are the Paralympics REALLY About? | Explained for Kids
snippet.description:
The Paralympic Games are some of the most inspiring sporting events in the world — but many people still don’t know how they began or why they exist.

In this Curious Professors current-events episode, Professor Punzworth explains what the Paralympics REALLY are, how they started after World War Two, and how athletes with disabilities compete at the highest levels of international sport — all in clear, kid-friendly language.

You’ll learn how a doctor named Ludwig Guttmann organized early sports competitions for injured veterans in 1948, how those small events grew into the global Paralympic Games, and how athletes compete in classification groups to ensure fair competition. Along the way, we explore winter Paralympic sports like para alpine skiing, para ice hockey, and wheelchair curling, and how the games help change the way the world thinks about ability and athletic achievement. A quick quiz and classroom discussion question wrap it all up!

snippet.title: What Medieval London Looked Like 6 Weeks Into the Black Death | A Week in 1348 (Day 7 — Finale)
snippet.description:
December 1348. Six weeks after the Black Death reached London, the city is still standing — but it has lost as much as half its people. This is the finale of A Week in Medieval London: seven days, seven lives, one city.

Not the kings and cathedrals — the apprentice running a workshop he wasn't ready for, the monk singing the office with seventeen empty choir stalls, the silk woman reopening her doors, the gravedigger at East Smithfield who stopped counting at two hundred, the alderman who keeps showing up, and the physician who keeps writing it all down.

We step back from the six lives we followed all week and look at the whole city — what life was really like in medieval London during the plague, what the city lost, what it kept, and why London is still here almost seven centuries later.

This is Day 7. And today, you are a survivor.

snippet.title: 7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London | 1348 Full Documentary
snippet.description:
7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London — the complete series in one full-length documentary.

In the autumn of 1348, the Black Death arrived in London. Within months it would kill between a third and a half of everyone in the city. This is the story of that catastrophe — not told through kings, battles, or cathedrals, but through seven ordinary people living one day at a time as the plague closed in around them.

Over roughly an hour and a half, you'll spend a full week inside medieval London in 1348: walking the cobbled streets of Cheapside, standing in the cold choir stalls of Westminster Abbey, sitting in a physician's candlelit workroom, and watching the long burial trenches grow at East Smithfield. This is immersive, historically grounded living-history — a reconstruction of what daily life, work, faith, medicine, and death actually looked like for medieval Londoners during the worst pandemic in European history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📜 WHAT YOU'LL SEE — THE FULL WEEK
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Day 1 — The Apprentice: a young weaver on Cheapside, watching the first death-carts roll past his master's workshop.
Day 2 —  The Monk
Day 3 — The Silk Woman: a craftswoman of Soper Lane fighting to keep her workshop and her trade alive as her workers fall ill.
Day 4 — The Gravedigger: a man at the East Smithfield burial ground who has stopped counting how many he has laid in the rows.
Day 5 — The Alderman: a ward official who keeps showing up to a half-empty Guildhall, quietly bending the rules to protect the living.
Day 6 — The Physician: a Montpellier-trained doctor with the wrong theory, the right instincts, and a notebook filling with the names of the dead.
Day 7 — The Survivor: the whole city, six weeks in — what London lost, what it kept, and why it is still here almost seven centuries later.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏰 ABOUT THIS SERIES
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
This is the complete "A Week in Medieval London (1348)" series from Time Warp Cities — a channel that reconstructs the daily texture of the past, one day, one life, and one city at a time. If you're fascinated by the Black Death, the bubonic plague, the Middle Ages, medieval England, and the real social history of how ordinary people lived, worked, and died, this full documentary is made for you.

We cover the history of the plague in London: how it spread along trade routes from Europe, why medieval medicine and miasma theory failed against it, what the East Smithfield mass burials reveal to archaeologists today, how the labour shortage that followed cracked the foundations of feudalism, and how the city survived and rebuilt — through 1348, the later plague returns, the Great Fire of 1666, and beyond.

snippet.title: The Falcata: The Deadliest Sword Before Rome
snippet.description:
What if one ancient sword was so powerful that it helped inspire one of the greatest weapons in history?

In this video, we explore the legendary Falcata, the iconic curved sword of the ancient Iberian warriors. Feared for its devastating cutting power, this remarkable weapon was used centuries before Roman rule and is believed to have influenced the design of the famous Roman gladius. Discover the history, craftsmanship, and battlefield impact of one of the most fascinating swords of the ancient world.
